title: Akka Mahadevi
hook: a woman at a stranger's door, hands held out, asking God that nothing be put in them: Akka Mahadevi's strangest request
tomorrow: Lal Ded — a season of the tradition's women

segments.voice: Yesterday, Akka Mahadevi in the hall at Kalyana, answering a hard question: the skin falls away when the fruit is ripe. Did you speak honestly about something still unfinished? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-two.

A woman goes from house to house with her hands held out. A wandering seeker, begging for her food. What's strange is what she asks for. She doesn't ask God to soften the hearts behind the doors. She asks for the doors to give her nothing. And if they do give, she asks for the food to fall. And if it falls, she asks for something even stranger. On our last day with Akka Mahadevi, one short poem, and a request that runs backward.
screen: `HOUSE TO HOUSE, HANDS OUT.` → `SHE ASKS FOR NOTHING.` → `A REQUEST THAT RUNS BACKWARD.`

segments.voice: Here is the vachana, in paraphrase. Make me go from house to house, hands held out for alms. If I beg, let them give me nothing. If they give, let it fall to the ground. If it falls, before I can pick it up, let a dog come and take it, O lord white as jasmine. Read it slowly and it works like a staircase going down. Each line takes away one more thing to lean on. First the comfort of home. Then the kindness of strangers. Then the food already in her hand. Then even the chance to stoop and pick it up. At the bottom of the stairs there is nothing left to hold, and the very last words are his name. That's the turn. The poem doesn't end on the dog. It ends on the lord white as jasmine. Readers in her own tradition, the Lingayat or Virashaiva way of Karnataka, hear in it the stripping away of every support but one. Some readers also hear a sharp honesty. She knows how easily a full plate becomes the thing she trusts. So she asks to be emptied, all the way, until the only thing in her hands is him. The poem never says she starves, and it never asks anyone else to live this way. It's one woman, talking to the one she loves, about what she's willing to let go. And there's a small surprise at the bottom of the staircase. A hungry dog eats. Even her emptiness feeds someone. Three days with Akka: a silkworm caught in its own threads, a hard question at the door of the saints, and, here, a woman asking for her hands to stay open.
screen: `A VACHANA ABOUT BEGGING` · `A STAIRCASE GOING DOWN` · `IT ENDS ON HIS NAME` · `HANDS LEFT OPEN`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open hands. Sit comfortably and let your hands rest in your lap, palms up, empty. Breathe slowly. Bring to mind one thing you lean on to feel steady today: a plan, a person's approval, a number in an account, a good night's sleep. Don't let go of it by force. Just notice how tightly you hold it. Then, with each breath out, let your palms soften a little more. If you pray, you can let the open hands be your prayer, without words. The bell holds the time.
Akka Mahadevi. The poet who asked God for her alms to fall, and for a dog to take them, and ended the poem on the name of the lord white as jasmine. Today's word.
Your line: Akka Mahadevi. Today, when something you were counting on doesn't come through, pause and notice what is still in your hands. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: In Karnataka, Akka Mahadevi is honored among the Lingayat (Virashaiva) saints, and her vachanas are sung, recited and taught in Kannada.

fork.setup: you're Akka in the poem. someone has given you food, and it slips from your hands to the ground. what do you ask for?

for a dog to take it before you can.
for the house to give you more.

notes: Written after reading days 1360 (the silkworm vachana) and 1361 (Kalyana and Allama Prabhu); this day takes a different vachana. The closing look-back summarizes those two days.

Vachana paraphrase: confirm the sequence (house to house begging; let them give nothing; if they give, let it fall; if it falls, let a dog take it before she picks it up) against the Kannada. Popular English versions are under copyright, so it is paraphrased.

Lingayat identity: some Lingayats regard their tradition as distinct from Hinduism. The script names her tradition as Lingayat or Virashaiva and makes no claim either way; a Keeper may want to word this.
Original: Kannada script ಅಕ್ಕ ಮಹಾದೇವಿ; confirm spelling and pronunciation. The guide prefers Devanagari for Hindu days, which does not fit a Kannada name.
The 'request that runs backward' framing and the staircase reading are the writer's; the readings attributed to her tradition and to 'some readers' should be checked by a Keeper.
Editor pass: fixed a garbled line that called the tradition's readers its saints.
